subject: principles-of-accounts
title: Absorption and Marginal Costing: Where the Fixed Overhead Goes

slides.heading: Absorption and Marginal Costing: Where the Fixed Overhead Goes
bullets: How one product cost is built under both methods: direct materials $10, direct labour $6 and variable overhead $4 land in both unit costs, fixed production overhead of $12 per unit lands only in the absorption unit cost, and because 1,000 units are produced but only 800 sold, the two profit figures separate by exactly the $2,400 of fixed overhead carried forward in closing inventory
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we build one product cost layer by layer under both methods and watch exactly where the fixed overhead goes.

slides.heading: What we will learn
bullets: Build both unit costs layer by layer: $20 marginal and $32 absorption

Explain why closing inventory of 200 units carries $2,400 of fixed overhead forward under absorption costing only, and why absorption profit of $9,400 exceeds marginal profit of $7,000 by exactly that amount
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud and tell the class: by the end you will be able to reconcile the two profit figures to the dollar.

slides.heading: Same factory, same sales - so why two different profits?
bullets: Both methods cost the same product, sell the same 800 units at $50, and face the same $12,000 of fixed production overhead
If nothing real differs, where can a $2,400 profit gap come from?
slides.notes: Ask the class: if both methods are honest, can they report different profits? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because the difference is timing, not truth.

slides.heading: The methods differ on timing - where the fixed overhead is charged
bullets: Marginal costing charges the full $12,000 of fixed production overhead to the period; its unit cost is the $20 variable cost only
Absorption costing attaches $12 of fixed overhead to each unit, so unsold units carry their share forward in closing inventory
When production exceeds sales, absorption defers part of the fixed overhead and reports the higher profit
slides.notes: Stress the deciding idea: fixed production overhead is a period cost under marginal costing but a product cost under absorption costing.

slides.heading: Both unit costs build from the same three variable layers
bullets: Direct materials $10, direct labour $6 and variable production overhead $4 land in both columns, layer by layer
Both methods agree so far: the variable cost of one unit is $20
slides.notes: Play scene 1 and point to the two columns growing together: nothing separates the methods yet.

slides.heading: Fixed overhead lands only in the absorption column
bullets: Fixed production overhead is $12,000 for 1,000 units produced, which is $12 per unit
That $12 layer lands only in the absorption column, taking its unit cost to $32, while marginal costing routes the $12,000 to the period as a whole
slides.notes: Play scene 2 and stop at the fork: the same $12,000 takes two different routes from this moment.

slides.heading: Closing inventory carries $2,400 of fixed overhead forward
bullets: The business produces 1,000 units but sells only 800, leaving 200 units in closing inventory
Under absorption costing each of those 200 units carries $12 of fixed overhead, so $2,400 is carried forward in inventory; under marginal costing the full $12,000 is expensed in this period
slides.notes: Play scene 3 and point to the closing inventory: the $2,400 has not vanished, it is sitting in the warehouse.

slides.heading: Absorption profit is higher by exactly that $2,400
bullets: Marginal costing gives a contribution of 800 x $30, minus $12,000 and $5,000, for a profit of $7,000
Absorption costing charges 800 x $32, giving a profit of $9,400 - higher by exactly the $2,400 deferred in inventory
slides.notes: Play scene 4 and watch the two profit bars: they differ by exactly the fixed overhead carried forward, no more and no less.

slides.heading: Worked example: reconciling the two profits
bullets: Marginal: revenue $40,000, contribution 800 x ($50 - $20) = $24,000, minus fixed overhead $12,000 and non-production costs $5,000 gives $7,000
Absorption: cost of sales 800 x $32 = $25,600, gross profit $14,400, minus $5,000 gives $9,400; the gap is 200 x $12 = $2,400
slides.notes: Work it slowly: Step 1, build both unit costs - $20 and $32. Step 2, compute closing inventory units - 200. Step 3, value the deferral - 200 x $12 = $2,400. Step 4, reconcile - $7,000 + $2,400 = $9,400.

slides.heading: Your turn: production 1,000, sales 900
bullets: In pairs: with the same costs, production of 1,000 units and sales of 900, state the closing inventory, the fixed overhead carried forward, and which method reports the higher profit
Then swap and check: did your partner multiply the 100 unsold units by the $12 fixed overhead per unit?
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes. Listen for the full chain, then take two pairs answers: closing inventory 100 units, deferral $1,200, absorption profit higher by $1,200.

slides.heading: Exit ticket: prove it before you leave
bullets: Your exit ticket asks you to correct a student who thinks the two methods must always report the same profit
Name where the fixed overhead goes under each method and reconcile the $2,400 gap to earn full credit
slides.notes: Point to the exit ticket and remind the class: the strongest answers track the $12 per unit into closing inventory.
